newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: African peacekeepers try to crush Bangui mutineers.
newsitem.headline: African peacekeepers try to crush Bangui mutineers.

text.p: Backed by heavy weaponry, African troops sent to bring peace to the Central African Republic are trying to crush resistance from disaffected soldiers after clashes in which at least 58 people died.

A lull on Tuesday evening followed a day in which shells, fired from tanks and mortars by the African force, thudded into southern suburbs controlled by mutineers, some of whom had not responded to a January peace deal to return to their units.

The death toll at the end of four days of clashes was at least 58 based on a Red Cross body count, while witnesses, whose stories tallied, gave a figure of at least 104 dead, according to local Red Cross head Doctor David Dofara.

There was no sign in the frightened city of Mali's widely respected former military leader, Amadou Toumani Toure, who brokered the January 25 agreement, and who on Monday said he was returning to Bangui.

The January peace deal the African force came to implement was preceded by three mutinies in less than a year in which political and ethnic supporters of President Ange-Felix Patasse in the army clashed with former comrades who became bitter enemies.

Thousands of people fled on Tuesday from homes in southern districts, close to the mutineers' stronghold at the Camp Kassai barracks, seeking safety in the north and west of the city with whatever belongings they could carry.
"This is to clean up pockets of resistance," said one officer in the African force, commenting on Tuesday's shelling.
The Red Cross is planning a camp for at least 8,000 people, who fled the first days of fighting. It has not yet explained what measures it will take to cope with the new exodus.

French troops are stationed in Bangui under a defence accord, but the former colonial power, which last year intervened to stop clashes, denied on Tuesday they were directly helping the African force.

After the latest fighting, Bangui's African force is looking less like a realistic model for bringing peace to Brazzaville, capital of the neighbouring Congo -- where it has been touted as a possible solution after over two weeks of sporadic clashes.

Mutinies in April and May 1996 in Bangui began as protests over pay but evolved into a movement to topple Patasse, a civilian from the north of the country elected in 1993. The third mutiny began in November and degenerated into ethnic bloodshed.
Most of the mutineers are members of the Yakoma tribe of former military leader Andre Kolingba.
The 800-strong African force includes soldiers from Burkina Faso, Chad, Gabon, Mali, Senegal and Togo. A Senegalese soldier killed on Friday was among the first casualties of the flare-up.
